h:
Anthropic has completed a record-breaking public listing that valued it at $2 trillion and could decide the future of the AI industry.

The IPO had been seen as a test of whether the vast amount of interest from the public and investors in artificial intelligence – as well as the big promises from the frontier AI companies themselves – would translate into a high valuation.

"I've looked at this whole week as a referendum on AI. Nvidia gave us a read on the buildout, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies," Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, said before the Anthropic debut.

Anthropic appears to have passed the test. The IPO valued it at $1.9 trillion, and it went even higher once trading started, as it launched on the Nasdaq, the biggest public listing in stock market history.

That comes alongside an even better earnings report from AI poster Child Nvidia on Tuesday. Taken together, the two suggest that the AI boom is set to continue – at least for now.

That didn’t always look so sure. The AI industry has been hit with a number of troubles in recent weeks – from warnings about the danger of the technology to US elections that brought the threat of greater regulation, as well as more unexpected events such as the ouster of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang from the company he founded.

But none of those troubles appeared to dampen interest in Anthropic’s flotation, or investing in AI more generally. Demand for Anthropic’s shares was even better than expected: it sold its shares at $83 each, above the initial range of $70 to $78 set as it began marketing it, and it traded up 31 per cent as the market opened.

But a public listing is just the beginning for Anthropic and for AI companies’ relationship with investors generally. There are a host of challenges on their way for frontier AI labs – and Anthropic’s status as the first of them to have shares publicly listed means that it will now be a way of reflecting, and betting on, how significant they could be.

What’s more, Anthropic and other companies will almost certainly come back to the financial markets to raise money for the vast amounts of money they are expected to need to keep building out data centres. "At some point in the future we're hoping to be investment grade, and debt is an instrument that we have ⁠available to us, and we'd like to use at some point in the future," chief executive Dario Amodei told CNBC in an interview around the IPO.

As such, Anthropic is going to need to be able to sustain the rapid growth that it allowed to command such a high valuation. And it will also need to be able to show that it can turn that growth into real profits, before investors become concerned that its high revenues will not turn into actual money.

Anthropic is already more focused on such work than other rivals, such as OpenAI, which is also hoping to pursue its own public listing. While OpenAI has focused primarily on growing its user base, Anthropic has aimed more at encouraging paid users for products such as Claude, as well as pushing them into businesses.

The company’s public status will also mean that it has to provide more details on its existing financing, as well as giving investors a way to express concern about them. Debate has intensified across global markets in recent months over whether the AI boom is veering into bubble territory, with economists, CEOs and political leaders split over its sustainability.

Much of the ‌scrutiny has focused on circular financing arrangements. A complicated web of deals between AI companies, chipmakers, cloud providers and investors has raised questions over how much of ​the industry's growth is being fuelled by money circulating within the same ecosystem.

Anthropic has nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google, underscoring how its rapid growth hinges on securing vast amounts of future computing capacity, some of ‌which relies on financing beyond the company's control.

Investors will ​be watching Anthropic's debut and subsequent trading closely, with analysts expecting the stock to emerge ‌as a proxy for the broader AI trade.

The company will also need to ​balance growth with calls to slow the development of advanced AI models. Anthropic warned in its IPO prospectus that AI could behave unpredictably and advance faster than oversight mechanisms.

Anthropic's listing is also set to create thousands of paper millionaires and a handful of billionaires. The vast amount of money flowing into the company has already prompted speculation about how it could change the AI industry, as well as the Bay Area that serves as its primary home.

Based on the IPO price, CEO Amodei and his six co-founders, who together own about 10 per cent of the company, had stakes valued at nearly $150 billion.

More broadly, the listing is expected to create a wave of new wealth across the AI sector, rewarding everyone from early researchers and engineers to administrative staff. It remains unclear how that money will be used – whether it could further add to a feeling of inequality in cities such as San Francisco and around the AI industry more generally, or if it could be used to fund philanthropic work that could help improve the public sentiment around artificial intelligence.
